Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "Please prepare a practical catalogue of the family photographs held by Mara Ellis and her brother, Daniel. They are sorting the collection before it is divided between their homes, and they want a shared record that will help relatives find pictures without requiring anyone to recognize every person in them. The collection contains about 640 prints and 90 digital images, mostly from the Ellis and Navarro sides of the family. It spans several generations, but the dates and names are uneven: some prints have notes on the back, some are in envelopes with partial labels, and many have no identifying information. Make the catalogue useful for family members who know the people and places, while keeping uncertainty visible rather than turning guesses into facts.

The oldest prints are believed to include photographs from the 1940s, though the earliest dated item is marked 1951. A group of pictures from a 1968 reunion in Yakima is labeled in Mara’s handwriting, and several envelopes refer to the Navarro family’s former grocery shop on Alder Street. There are also albums from Daniel’s childhood in the 1970s and 1980s, loose school portraits, holiday snapshots, and recent phone photographs. Treat these descriptions as leads for organizing the material, not as proof that every photograph in a group shows the same people or event. The family would like to retain the original order of albums and envelopes wherever possible, since that arrangement sometimes carries useful context.

Build the record around individual photographs or clearly bounded groups when a set is genuinely part of one event. Include a stable catalogue number, a short description, the best available date or date range, the source album or envelope, and any people or locations that can be identified with confidence. Note whether an item is a print or digital image and record any legible writing on the back or in the original file name. When a caption is supplied by a relative, identify who supplied it and keep their wording distinct from your own description. A relative’s recollection can be helpful even when it is tentative; show its status plainly rather than silently adopting it as confirmed metadata.

1. Use the original physical arrangement as the starting point. Give albums, envelopes, and digital folders source labels that are easy to distinguish, and record the original page or position when it can be observed without dismantling an album. If a loose print has no known source, mark the source as unknown instead of assigning it to the nearest album. Keep duplicate prints connected by cross-reference, but do not treat them as separate moments unless the images show a meaningful difference. The catalogue should let Mara and Daniel locate an item again after the collection is split, so include a simple location field that they can fill in once they decide where each original will live.

2. Use dates at the level supported by the evidence. If a photograph has a reliable date written on it or embedded in its digital file, record that date and indicate the source. If the evidence supports only a period, use a range such as “circa 1974–1976” and explain briefly what supports it. If a date cannot reasonably be estimated, write “date unknown”; do not infer one from clothing, image quality, or a relative’s age alone. Where two plausible dates remain in disagreement, retain both as attributed possibilities instead of choosing between them. Apply the same care to names and places: distinguish an identification offered by a family member from one confirmed by a label or other clear evidence.

Mara can identify her mother, Elena Navarro, in most of the reunion photographs, and Daniel recognizes their uncle Peter Ellis in a number of the shop pictures. They are less certain about the people standing behind the counter in two undated prints. Mara thinks one woman may be their great-aunt Rosa, while Daniel remembers hearing that Rosa moved away before the shop closed. Record those differing recollections as attributed possibilities; do not resolve them by choosing one account. A handwritten note on an envelope reads, “Alder Street, before the new sign went up.” Preserve that wording as a transcription, including its uncertainty about when the sign changed, and do not present it as a precise date or a confirmed description of a particular print.

The shared catalogue should be easy to maintain in a spreadsheet or similar table, with one row per item or carefully defined group and consistent fields throughout. Include a brief note explaining the meaning of any labels used for confidence, attribution, or missing information. Avoid specialist archival terms unless they are explained in ordinary language. The catalogue is for family use rather than public display, so keep personal context concise and relevant to identifying or locating photographs. Do not add sensitive family stories that are not needed for that purpose. Where a photograph includes people who may still be living, describe them respectfully and avoid publishing contact details or other private information.

Please provide the catalogue plan in three parts: first, a concise description of the proposed fields and how the uncertainty labels work; second, a small illustrative sample using only the facts in this request, with no invented dates or identifications; and third, a short set of practical steps for Mara and Daniel to continue cataloguing the remaining material. In the sample, use the 1968 reunion label, the two shop photographs with disputed identifications, and the envelope note as examples where appropriate. Do not claim to have inspected images or originals. If a sample field cannot be filled from the supplied information, show it as unknown or explain that it needs checking rather than supplying a plausible value.

For the work process, suggest how the siblings can compare notes without overwriting one another’s recollections. They expect to work in two sessions at Mara’s house, using a laptop and a phone to enter notes while handling the prints. Recommend a straightforward way to record who made an identification and when, and a way to flag items that need a second look. Keep the steps realistic for two people working with ordinary household supplies; they have not selected scanning equipment or a permanent storage system. Do not turn this into a digitization or conservation project, though brief handling advice may be included if it directly helps them avoid mixing or damaging the photographs.

Mara and Daniel would like to finish the initial catalogue before their cousin Lena visits in June, because she may recognize people from the Navarro side. Make the plan flexible enough to leave some records incomplete until Lena has reviewed them. The final catalogue should make clear which information is supported by an object or file, which comes from a named person’s memory, and which remains unresolved.
